elements.quote: As this study is underpowered to investigate the underlying mechanism of these inflammatory markers with the severity of COVID-19, further studies aiming at analyzing pathophysiological mechanisms of COVID-19 are needed. We also examined evidence of publication bias in our meta-analyses, and the presence of non-reporting bias was suggested in the meta-analysis on the association of IL-6 with severity. ... Different definitions of the term 'severity' adopted by each author, some variables such as the time taken to collect laboratory tests or the number of the days from symptoms onset of COVID-19 to hospital admission may also have notably contributed to this circumstance. Discrepancies in reporting and detailing patients' comorbidities in each study may also have reinforced heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The limitations section explicitly describes current uncertainties and limitations in the evidence base (heterogeneity, underpowered to investigate mechanisms, population generalizability, variable definitions), which addresses the current state of knowledge and important uncertainties.

elements.quote: We believe that the results of our review and meta-analysis including a relevant number of patients, especially those related to IL-6 and ferritin, can be extrapolated to the real world, supporting clinical practice in coping with COVID-19 and may help decision-making processes. As this is a living review, we are committed to keeping it updated as new evidence is published.
elements.reason: The authors state the review's potential to support clinical practice and decision-making and commit to updating it, explaining the importance and need for conducting the review.
No provided evidence explains the need for the current review in the context of prior similar systematic reviews or cites/updates previous reviews.

elements.quote: Eligible studies were those including laboratory parameters-including serum interleukin-6 levels-from mild, moderate, or severe COVID-19 cases. Laboratory parameters, such as interleukin-6, ferritin, hematology, C-Reactive Protein, procalcitonin, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, creatinine, and D-dimer, were extracted from the studies.
elements.reason: This review assesses laboratory biomarkers (observational studies) rather than interventions; a description of an intervention mechanism is therefore not applicable.

elements.quote: Eligible studies were those including laboratory parameters-including serum interleukin-6 levels-from mild, moderate, or severe COVID-19 cases. Laboratory parameters, such as interleukin-6, ferritin, hematology, C-Reactive Protein, procalcitonin, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, creatinine, and D-dimer, were extracted from the studies.
elements.reason: The review concerns biomarker measurement from observational studies rather than complex interventions or delivery contexts; a logic model for intervention components is therefore not applicable.

elements.quote: To describe the laboratory parameters and biomarkers of the cytokine storm syndrome associated with severe and fatal COVID-19 cases.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated (to describe laboratory parameters and biomarkers associated with severe and fatal COVID-19), but it is not framed using a recognized question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, PECOS) as required by this element.

elements.quote: The main limitations of this review stem from the nature of the included studies; all included studies were observational as they were published with the inherent urgency of a global pandemic.
elements.reason: This element applies to reviews of intervention effects (requiring PICO-style planned comparisons). The review is based on observational studies of biomarkers (not intervention effects), so the conditional requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they presented laboratory data-including serum IL-6 levels-from mild-to-moderate, severe or critical patients with COVID-19, according to the National Health Commission of China (NHCC) Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of COVID-19 [8] or World Health Organization Interim Guidance for COVID-19 [9]. Exclusion criteria consisted of studies that assessed pregnant women, pediatric patients, individuals co-infected with other microorganisms, or populations exclusively related to oncological, rheumatological, transplants, or chronic renal disease.
elements.reason: The eligibility criteria specify included study characteristics (laboratory data including IL-6, severity categories per NHCC/WHO) and list excluded populations (pregnant, pediatric, co-infected, oncology, rheumatology, transplants, chronic renal disease), fulfilling the requirement to report study characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: All studies published before November 28 th , 2020 were included, and no language restrictions were implemented for electronic search.
elements.reason: The review specifies the publication cutoff date (studies published before Nov 28, 2020) and explicitly states no language restrictions, addressing report characteristics (date and language).

elements.quote: We retrieved 136 full-text articles for further scrutiny; of those, 96 studies were excluded due to: ineligible population(n = 10), study design (n = 5), different definition of severity (n = 11) or not reporting the laboratory data of interest for this meta-analysis (n = 70) (S3 Table).
elements.reason: The review distinguishes exclusion for 'not reporting the laboratory data of interest' (i.e., results not reported), but does not explicitly distinguish or state exclusions because outcomes were not measured versus not reported; thus partly addresses the criterion.

elements.quote: Studies were assessed into two separate groups for analysis: severity group and mortality group. Laboratory parameters, such as IL-6, ferritin, hemoglobin, leukocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, platelets, CRP, procalcitonin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), creatinine, and D-dimer were analyzed.
elements.reason: The review specifies the groups used for synthesis (severity group and mortality group) and links them to the comparisons/objectives by listing the laboratory parameters analyzed within those syntheses.

Although exclusion criteria are listed (e.g., pregnant, pediatric, co-infected, certain disease populations), the manuscript does not provide explicit rationales explaining why these notable restrictions on eligibility were applied.

elements.quote: Asearch with standardized descriptors and synonyms was performed on November 28 th , 2020 of the MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, LILACS, and IBECS to identify studies of interest.
elements.reason: An explicit search date (November 28, 2020) is reported for the information sources searched.

elements.quote: Wesearched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), LILACS, and IBECS using relevant descriptors and synonyms, adapting the search to the specifics of each database (S1 Table).
elements.reason: The bibliographic databases are named, but no search interface/platform or coverage dates for each database are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: We also searched the Open Grey database, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov to identify published, ongoing, and unpublished studies.
elements.reason: Study registers/repositories are named (WHO ICTRP, ClinicalTrials.gov, Open Grey), but the evidence does not report any date restrictions specific to these sources (only an overall search date is provided).

elements.quote: We also searched the Open Grey database, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov to identify published, ongoing, and unpublished studies.
elements.reason: Names of online sources are provided (e.g., Open Grey), but no URLs or detailed identification (such as exact search engine names with URLs) are reported in the provided evidence.
No evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies; the manuscript mentions contacting study authors but not organisations or manufacturers.

elements.quote: We attempted to contact the authors of the included studies when any study data or other details were missing.
elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted (authors of included studies) are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Finally, we used the technique of snowballing, searching the lists of references of the included studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies that reference lists of the included studies were examined (i.e., lists of references of included studies).

elements.quote: Nineteen studies assessed fatal and non-fatal groups of patients with COVID-19 and reported IL-6. Pooled results from these studies showed that the patients who progressed to death had higher levels of IL-6 in comparison with those who survived [MD 70.82; 95% CI 45.24 to 96.41; N = 5,229] (Fig 2A). Pooled results from twenty-two studies of both severe and nonsevere cases revealed higher levels of Il-6 in patients with severe COVID-19 in comparison to the group of mild COVID-19 cases [MD 28.99; 95% CI 18.24 to 39.75; N = 4,861] (Fig 2B). The pooled analysis of nine studies showed that patients with COVID-19 who did not survive also had higher levels of ferritin [MD 853.43; 95% CI 601.20 to 1105.67; N = 2,088] (Fig 2C). elements.quote: In this living systematic review with meta-analysis, a clear pattern of hematological, biochemical, inflammatory, and immune biomarker abnormalities could be found between patients with or without severe disease. These differences could allow for the identification of predictors of severe and fatal cases. We found that lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and high levels of ferritin, D-dimer, aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase, C-Reactive Protein, neutrophils, procalcitonin and creatinine are good indicators of both severe and fatal cases of COVID-19 during the first days from illness onset, as is interleukin-6, the main cytokine involved in the CSS. ... This result is consistent with those reported by Chen G et al. [16], who demonstrated that the total lymphocyte count, and specifically CD4 + T cells and CD8+ T cells, were slightly lower in moderate cases and significantly decreased in severe COVID-19. This study concluded that the cytokine storm is associated with COVID19 severity, likely through increased pulmonary pathology, T cell depletion, and CD4+ T cell dysfunction. Our meta-analysis also found an association between lymphopenia and higher mortality. ... Another meta-analysis showed a similar result of the discriminatory ability of D-dimer in patients with and without severe forms of COVID-19 but did not provide data on mortality [71].
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly interprets the review's findings and compares them with findings from other studies and prior meta-analyses (e.g., Chen G et al. and another meta-analysis on D-dimer), placing results in the context of existing evidence.

elements.quote: The main limitations of this review stem from the nature of the included studies; all included studies were observational as they were published with the inherent urgency of a global pandemic. Although these are study designs with a lower level of evidence, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessment of the risk of bias of the included studies did not show any salient risks. Another chief limitation lies in the fact that most patients are of Asian origin, which may compromise the external validity of this meta-analysis. Assessing the statistical heterogeneity of the included studies is an essential component of interpreting the results of any meta-analysis. In the present study, the meta-analysis of most outcomes showed considerable heterogeneity, requiring a more detailed examination of the studies in order to determine possible causes for this issue. We attempted to explore sources of statistical heterogeneity by thoroughly examining clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies and by performing sensitivity analysis. While we explored the sources of heterogeneity in the meta-analyses, we could not find differences that could explain the sources of heterogeneity across studies. As the clinical course of patients with COVID-19 may widely vary across individuals, unexplored clinical parameters may explain this heterogeneity. Different definitions of the term 'severity' adopted by each author, some variables such as the time taken to collect laboratory tests or the number of the days from symptoms onset of COVID-19 to hospital admission may also have notably contributed to this circumstance. Discrepancies in reporting and detailing patients' comorbidities in each study may also have reinforced heterogeneity. Although considerable, the heterogeneity does not compromise the robustness of this meta-analysis, as it did not interfere with the direction and the magnitude of effects. As this study is underpowered to investigate the underlying mechanism of these inflammatory markers with the severity of COVID-19, further studies aiming at analyzing pathophysiological mechanisms of COVID-19 are needed. Wealso examined evidence of publication bias in our meta-analyses, and the presence of non-reporting bias was suggested in the meta-analysis on the association of IL-6 with severity. As we found important heterogeneity in this meta-analysis and tests for adjusting for funnel plot asymmetry such as the trim and fill method are known to perform poorly when there is large between-study heterogeneity [78], we did not perform trim and fill test. Of note, smallstudy effects may be due to reasons other than publication bias, such as heterogeneity [6]. It is likely that asymmetry in this meta-analysis is also due to heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly discusses multiple limitations of the included evidence: observational study designs, geographic (Asian) patient predominance affecting external validity, considerable statistical heterogeneity across outcomes, inability to identify sources of heterogeneity, variable definitions of severity and timing of measurements, discrepancies in comorbidity reporting, and possible publication/non-reporting bias.

Our review demonstrated that older age, male gender, and comorbidities represent potential risk factors for severe and fatal cases, as has already been reported in the scientific literature.
